title: Tenant scaling scenarios, SLA decomposition, and on‑call escalation matrix
author: Priya N. Reddy
body:
Overview

Purpose: This document captures common tenant scaling scenarios observed in Redwood Private deployments, decomposes tenant-facing SLAs into measurable SLOs, and defines an operator-friendly on-call escalation matrix and runbook for day‑2 incidents. It is intended for field operators, SREs, and solutions engineers responsible for Private (VPC / on‑prem) customers.

Scope:
- Applies to multi-tenant and single-tenant Private deployments managed by Redwood operators or customer operators using Redwood Private.
- Covers traffic/load patterns, autoscale behavior, throttling/quotas, monitoring signals, alert thresholds, and escalation steps.
- Does not replace customer-specific contractual SLAs; use this as the operational implementation reference.

Key definitions
- Tenant: logical customer workload (customer account, namespace, or project).
- Capacity headroom: spare GPU / worker capacity reserved for unexpected bursts.
- KV cache hit: prefix / KV cache hit used to reduce token compute.

1) SLA decomposition and measurable SLOs

| SLA objective | Decomposed SLO | Monitoring signal | Alert threshold | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| End-user response latency | P95 inference latency per-tenant < 350 ms | per-tenant latency histogram (P95) | P95 > 350 ms for 5m | Tenant owner (ops) / Redwood SRE |
| Availability (serving) | Error rate < 0.1% over 1h | 5xx / user errors per 1k requests | error rate > 0.1% for 15m | Platform SRE |
| Throughput | Sustained throughput capacity >= committed TPS | per-tenant request/sec | sustained drop below 90% of committed for 10m | Capacity planning team |
| Quality regressions | Model regression rate vs baseline < 2% on eval prompt set | automatic evals tied to deployment | regression detected on rolling deploy | Model onboarding / Product |

Rationale and headroom guidance
- Default headroom: reserve 20% of provisioned GPU capacity for safety margin in multi-tenant clusters.
- For enterprise SLA customers, bump reserve to 35% and configure burst pool routing to dedicated nodes.

2) Tenant scaling scenarios (patterns & operator expectations)

A. Gradual growth
- Description: sustained increase in request rate over hours/days.
- Expected behavior: autoscaler increases worker replicas gradually (scale-up cooldown 5m).
- Operator actions: verify synthetic traffic tests, ensure model quantization profile applied, monitor KV cache warming.

B. Short burst (traffic spike)
- Description: sudden spike over 10s–2m (e.g., viral event).
- Expected behavior: autoscaler cannot react instantly; short-term throttling or token-burst bucket enforces limits; fallback models served if configured.
- Operator actions: verify burst pool availability, temporarily increase burst capacity or engage failover routing.

C. Noisy neighbor (one tenant saturates shared resources)
- Description: single tenant consumes disproportionate GPU or I/O causing other tenants to see latency spikes.
- Expected behavior: tenant-level quotas and circuit breakers should limit impact.
- Operator actions: enforce tenant qps/rt limits, evict or throttle offending tenant, open customer incident if contractual.

3) Alerting and monitoring signals (examples)
- Primary metrics to instrument per tenant: p50/p95/p99 latency, request rate, error rate, queue depth, KV cache hit rate, GPU utilization, memory pressure, disk I/O latency.
- Secondary signals: model load (KV cache size), batching efficiency (avg batch size), quantization downshifts.

Suggested Prometheus-style alerts (pseudo YAML)

ALERT TenantP95LatencyHigh
  IF increase(per_tenant_p95_latency_seconds[5m]) > 0 AND per_tenant_p95_latency_seconds > 0.35
  FOR 5m
  LABELS { severity = "page" }
  ANNOTATIONS { summary = "Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} P95 > 350ms" }

ALERT TenantErrorRateHigh
  IF rate(per_tenant_errors_total[5m]) / rate(per_tenant_requests_total[5m]) > 0.001
  FOR 10m
  LABELS { severity = "ticket" }
  ANNOTATIONS { summary = "Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} error rate > 0.1%" }

ALERT TenantKVCacheCold
  IF per_tenant_kv_cache_hit_rate < 0.6
  FOR 15m
  LABELS { severity = "warn" }
  ANNOTATIONS { summary = "Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} KV cache hit rate < 60%" }

4) On-call escalation matrix and severity definitions

Severity mapping:
- Sev 1 (page): widespread production impact (large portion of traffic broken, SLO violated, revenue impact). Immediate page to on-call SRE + product on-call.
- Sev 2 (page + follow-up): degraded latency/throughput for a single major tenant or multiple tenants. Page the platform on-call.
- Sev 3 (ticket): localized, non-urgent issues (minor errors, config drift). Create a ticket for engineering queue.

Escalation matrix (operator-friendly):
1. First responder: Platform on-call (SRE) — investigate dashboards, run retros, check autoscaler and burst pool.
2. If not resolved in 15 minutes: Page Runtime Engineering (serving-runtime team).
3. If not resolved in 45 minutes: Page Product on-call / customer success for customer comms.
4. If SLA breach imminent or regulatory impact: Page Security & Compliance.

Contact list (examples):
- Platform on-call: #redwood-oncall (PagerDuty)
- Runtime engineering: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Product on-call: product-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Customer Success escalation: cs-esc@redwood.example.com

5) Runbook: Immediate triage steps (ordered)
1. Acknowledge page and set Slack channel + incident docs page.
2. Identify scope: single tenant vs multi-tenant (query per-tenant metrics).
3. Check autoscaler events and recent deploys (last 60 minutes).
4. Verify KV cache hit rate and warm-up state.
5. Inspect GPU utilization and queue depths. Are there nodes under OOM or high thermal throttling?
6. If noisy neighbor detected: apply tenant throttle, scale down offending tenant, and re-balance workloads (commands below).
7. If capacity shortage: if burst pool exists, move affected traffic to burst nodes. If not, engage capacity allocation run (contact capacity planner).
8. If model regression suspected: revert to previous model version, or activate rollback tag for model package.
9. Monitor metrics after mitigation for 30 minutes, then update incident timeline and notify stakeholders.

Example operator CLI snippets (abstracted)
- Throttle tenant qps: rwmctl tenant throttle --tenant-id T-123 --qps 20 --duration 30m
- Move traffic to burst pool: rwmctl route-override --tenant-id T-123 --target burst-pool --weight 100
- Revert model version: rwmctl model promote --tenant-id T-123 --model-version v2.14.3

6) Configuration examples and safe defaults

| Setting | Default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| autoscaler.cooldown_seconds | 300 | prevents flapping during transient spikes |
| tenant.qps_limit_default | 100 | conservative default for shared clusters |
| burst_pool.capacity_pct | 10% | percent of total cluster reserved as burst pool |
| kv_cache.target_hit_rate | 0.75 | target to justify optimistic KV caching |

7) Canary scale/runbook for rolling scale changes and upgrades
Purpose: safely increase cluster capacity or change autoscaler parameters with minimal customer impact.

Steps:
1. Identify low-traffic tenants for canary (>= 2 tenants preferred).
2. Apply autoscaler parameter change to canary tenants only.
3. Monitor primary signals for 30–60 minutes. If P95 increases < 5% and error rate unchanged, widen to 10% of tenants.
4. If any regression detected, roll back parameter for canary tenants immediately and open a regression investigation.
5. After gradual rollout to 100% and 24h validation, commit change to cluster config.

8) Post-incident actions and continuous improvement
- Required artifacts: timeline, root cause hypothesis, mitigation steps, customer impact summary, follow-up actions with owners and deadlines.
- Suggested retro cadence: monthly review of tenant incidents and capacity anomalies; update default headroom and throttling defaults based on trends.

9) Ownership and run adoption plan
- Primary owners: Platform SRE (operational alerts), Runtime Engineering (behavioural fixes), Capacity Planning (long-term headroom), Customer Success (customer comms).
- Adoption plan: include these SLOs and runbook steps in new private-deploy onboarding checklist; schedule tabletop drills quarterly with the field team.

10) Related artifacts and references
- Private deploy onboarding runbook (see related_pages).
- Runtime observability mapping (see related_pages).
